 "summary": "Configures the Nix Windows cross-compilation shell to build GCC with the POSIX thread model rather than the default MCF model, aligning CI with Guix release binaries. The PR also raises the Docker BuildKit step log limit to 5 MiB and logs the compiler configuration in CI before running tests.",
 "problem": "Nix Windows cross builds in CI used GCC's MCF thread model while Guix release binaries use POSIX threads, causing CI to test binaries with different threading runtimes and dependencies than production builds. <category name="build" title="Build and CI">
## Covers

How the project is built, tested, and released: the CMake build system,
the depends system and its packages, Guix reproducible builds, CI
configuration and scripts, compiler and platform support, and the
tooling under contrib used for releases and development. Platform
labels (Windows, macOS) point here when the change is about building or
running on that platform rather than about a feature. The Build system
label is a strong prior.

Not build: source changes that happen to fix a compiler warning as a
side effect (they belong to their area).

## What matters here

Release integrity first: reproducibility of Guix builds, correctness of
dependency pinning and verification, and anything that could ship a
wrong binary. Then supported-platform breakage: a platform that fails
to build or run blocks users on it. Then CI reliability: flaky or
misleading jobs waste every contributor's time and hide real failures.
Then dependency transitions with deadlines (compiler or library minimum
versions, deprecations upstream). Then build time and contributor
friction.

Cosmetic CMake cleanups rank low unless they remove a recurring
breakage.

<category name="tests" title="Test infrastructure">
## Covers

The machinery of testing rather than tests of a particular area: the
functional test framework and runner, unit test utilities, the fuzzing
harnesses and corpora, benchmarks, linters, sanitizer configuration,
and fixes for flaky tests whose cause is in the framework. A test that
pins the behavior of one area (a wallet migration test, a p2p relay
test) belongs to that area, not here. The Tests and Fuzzing labels are
a prior, but a labeled PR whose tests are about one area goes to that
area instead.

## What matters here

Signal first: fixes for flaky or misleading tests, since a red CI that
nobody trusts hides real failures. Then coverage of high-risk code paths
that the fuzzers or functional tests do not reach, especially
consensus, mempool policy, and p2p message handling. Then framework
capabilities that unblock tests other areas need. Then test speed, which
every contributor pays for on every run. Then cleanliness of the test
code.

Adding tests for their own sake ranks low; adding a test that catches a
realistic regression ranks high.

hint matches: {"labels": ["Tests"]}
</category>

<category name="tools" title="Tools and scripts">
## Covers

Command-line tools other than the node and its RPC client, and the
scripts under contrib: `bitcoin-tx`, `bitcoin-util`, the offline
`bitcoin-wallet` tool, the `bitcoin` wrapper, seed and asmap
generation, signet tooling, tracing scripts, and developer helper
scripts. Build and release scripts are build; test helpers are tests.
The Scripts and tools label is a strong prior.

## What matters here

Tools that operators and downstream projects depend on first: seed
generation, asmap, signet, and the wallet tool affect real deployments.
Then correctness of any tool that touches keys or transactions. Then
developer productivity tools that many contributors use. Then niche or
single-user scripts, which rank low regardless of size.
